subChunks.title: Scholarly Citation & Evidence Explained

storyBeats.txt: A citation is not a formality, Theodora said. It is an act of intellectual honesty. It tells your reader: here is exactly where I found this. Go and check it. I am not asking you to take my word for anything.

The difference between genealogical citation and academic citation in other disciplines is that genealogists work with an almost infinite variety of source types — civil registration, manorial court rolls, DNA company databases, family bibles, oral history recordings, microfilmed records of records that no longer exist. Each requires a different format.

Elizabeth Shown Mills spent twenty years codifying the templates. The result is Evidence Explained — a book that most genealogists find impenetrable the first time and indispensable the second. Master it.

subChunks.hookHtml:
Citation is the infrastructure of scholarship. Without it, every claim is unverifiable. Every argument is unchallengeable. Every error is invisible. In fields with a strong scholarly tradition — history, law, medicine — citation standards have evolved over centuries to ensure that knowledge is cumulative, verifiable, and correctable.

Genealogy developed its own citation standard relatively recently, but the intellectual case for it is identical. When Elizabeth Shown Mills published Evidence Explained in 2007, she systematised citation templates for thousands of genealogical source types. The book is now the professional standard, used by BCG portfolio applicants, NGSQ authors, and practitioners writing reports for probate courts. Understanding its logic — not just its templates — makes you a better researcher as well as a better writer.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Architecture of a Genealogical Citation

Every genealogical citation has the same logical structure, regardless of source type:

  1. Creator: Who created the source? (Author, institution, government body)
  2. Title: What is the source called?
  3. Date/Edition: When was it created or published?
  4. Specifics: What specific part of the source? (Volume, page, entry, folio, frame)
  5. Repository: Where is it held? (Archive, library, website)
  6. Access: How was it accessed? (Original, microfilm, digital image via platform; date accessed if online)

This structure holds whether the source is a 16th-century parish register, an 1881 census return, a DNA match on AncestryDNA, or an oral history interview. The specific elements vary; the logic does not.

First Reference vs. Subsequent Reference Citations

Evidence Explained provides templates for both first-reference citations (full, complete citations used the first time a source is mentioned) and subsequent-reference citations (shortened forms used thereafter). In reports, the first reference is typically in a footnote or endnote; subsequent references use an abbreviated form.

Example — GRO civil registration:

First reference: England & Wales Birth Registration, Northampton district, March quarter 1855, vol. 15, p. 43; General Register Office, Southport; digital image, Ancestry (www.ancestry.co.uk), accessed 14 April 2025.

Subsequent reference: GRO Birth Registration, Northampton, March 1855, vol. 15:43.

Citing Original vs. Derivative Sources

Citation should indicate whether the researcher is working from the original document, a microfilm copy, a digital image, or a transcription/abstract. This matters because the reliability of what was seen differs across these forms:

  • Original: 'St Mary's Church, Warwick, baptism register, 1803, entry for John Hall; original record at Warwickshire County Record Office.'
  • Microfilm: '...microfilm 1234567, frame 45; Family History Library, Salt Lake City.'
  • Digital image: '...digital image, Ancestry (www.ancestry.co.uk), accessed 14 April 2025.'
  • Transcription only: '...transcription, FindMyPast; original record not personally examined.'

The last form — where only a transcription has been seen — should prompt the researcher to note that the transcription's accuracy has not been independently verified against the original.

Citing DNA Evidence

DNA evidence requires citation like any other source. Elements to include: testing company and product (AncestryDNA autosomal test); tester's name or alias; match name or alias; cM amount shared; date of comparison; any tree or profile information associated with the match. Example:

'AncestryDNA autosomal test, kit for [Client Name]; match '[Match Name]', shared DNA 245 cM, predicted relationship 2nd–3rd cousin; tree attached showing [relevant ancestral surname]; Ancestry.com, accessed 15 April 2025.'

Citing Oral History and Family Tradition

Oral history and family tradition are valid genealogical sources, but their evidential weight is often secondary. Citation elements: informant (who said it); recipient (who recorded it); date of communication; medium (spoken, written, email); any supporting documentation. Example:

'Mary Smith (b. 1942, London), oral communication to [researcher name], 12 March 2025; relating family tradition that maternal grandmother came from County Clare, Ireland. No documentary evidence yet located to corroborate or refute this claim.'

Evidence Explained as a Reference Work

Evidence Explained: Citing History Sources from Artifacts to Cyberspace (Elizabeth Shown Mills, 3rd ed., 2015) provides citation templates for: vital records (birth, marriage, death); census records; land and property records; court records; military records; immigration records; church records; DNA databases; online databases; manuscript collections; and many more. It is organised by source category; each chapter begins with a discussion of the source type before providing templates. The discussion is itself valuable for understanding what the source is and how it was created.

The book is available from Genealogical Publishing Company. Elizabeth Shown Mills also maintains QuickLesson articles (at Evidence Explained: Historic Analysis, Credits and Citation, evidenceexplained.com) addressing citation questions not covered in the book.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why the same genealogical citation looks different depending on whether you're looking at the original document, a scanned image online, or just a transcription of someone else's reading.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: Construct full first-reference citations for each of the following: (1) You viewed a digital image of the 1871 England census on Ancestry — the entry is for James Hartley, Huddersfield sub-district, reference RG10/4541/82/6. (2) You found a baptism for Thomas Green in the Wakefield parish register on microfilm at the Family History Library, Salt Lake City, film number 1068471, frame 215, entry dated 15 March 1832. (3) A cousin told you by email on 3 June 2025 that your great-grandmother came from Galway — she had heard this from her father. (4) You found your client's DNA match 'JSmith_1234' on AncestryDNA, sharing 312 cM, with a public tree showing the Smith family of Sheffield.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) England & Wales Census 1871, Huddersfield sub-district, Yorkshire, household of James Hartley; RG10/4541/82/6; digital image, Ancestry (www.ancestry.co.uk), accessed [date].

(2) Wakefield Parish Church (St Peter's), Yorkshire, baptism register, entry for Thomas Green, 15 March 1832; original held at West Yorkshire Archive Service, Wakefield; microfilm 1068471, frame 215; Family History Library, Salt Lake City, Utah.

(3) [Cousin's name] (b. [year], [location]), email communication to [researcher name], 3 June 2025; reporting family tradition, received from her father, that maternal great-grandmother came from Galway, Ireland. No documentary evidence yet located to corroborate. Secondary information; original informant deceased.

(4) AncestryDNA autosomal test, kit for [client name]; match 'JSmith_1234', shared DNA 312 cM, predicted relationship 2nd cousin; public tree attached to match showing Smith family of Sheffield; Ancestry.com, accessed [date].
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: You are helping a colleague who is writing a report. They have written the following citation: 'Found in Irish records on FindMyPast — death of Patrick Nolan, 1887.' Identify every deficiency in this citation and write a corrected, professionally adequate version. Then explain why each missing element matters to a researcher who might want to verify the source.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Deficiencies in the original: (1) No indication of which type of record (civil registration? church record? workhouse death register?). (2) No registration district, county, or reference number. (3) 'FindMyPast' is a platform, not a source — it is the access route, not the original record. (4) No volume or entry number. (5) No indication of whether the original was viewed or only a transcription. (6) No access date. (7) 'Found in Irish records' is not a record type.

Corrected citation (assuming civil registration): Ireland Civil Registration Deaths, district of [district name], year 1887, vol. [X], p. [Y], entry for Patrick Nolan; General Register Office, Dublin; digital image via FindMyPast (www.findmypast.co.uk), accessed [date].

Why each element matters: The record type tells a future researcher where to look. The district and reference enable location of the exact same entry. The GRO Dublin identifies the authoritative repository. The platform and date of access note that a digital image was viewed (not the original) and when — relevant if the database is subsequently corrected or the image replaced. Without these elements, 'Irish records on FindMyPast — death of Patrick Nolan, 1887' could refer to any of dozens of different record types and cannot be independently verified or challenged.
learningObjectives: Describe the six-element logical structure underlying all genealogical citations.
Construct full first-reference citations for civil registration, census, church register, microfilm, digital image, DNA match, and oral history sources.
Distinguish between original, microfilm, digital image, and transcription-only access and explain why this distinction matters in citations.
Navigate Evidence Explained to find citation templates for unfamiliar source types.
commonMistakes: Citing the platform (Ancestry, FindMyPast) as the source rather than the underlying record it hosts.
Omitting the access date for online sources — databases change, images are added or corrected, and the date of access matters.
Using 'ibid.' or similar shorthand without establishing a clear first-reference citation that it can refer back to.
Treating transcription-only access the same as original-document access in citations.
assessmentCriteria: Citations include all required elements (creator, title, date, specifics, repository, access) for each source type.
Distinction between original, microfilm, digital image, and transcription is clearly reflected in the citation.
DNA citations include match name, cM amount, platform, and access date.
Oral history citations identify informant, recipient, date, medium, and the secondary nature of the information.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Elizabeth Shown Mills's online resource for citation and evidence analysis questions, complementing the printed third edition (2015) with QuickLessons on specific citation challenges.
Short online articles by Elizabeth Shown Mills addressing specific citation and evidence analysis questions not fully covered in the book — an invaluable supplement for unfamiliar source types.
An abbreviated citation form used after the first full reference to a source — shortens the footnote without losing the ability to locate the original full citation.
The repository is the archive or institution that holds the original record; the platform (Ancestry, FindMyPast, FamilySearch) is the digital access route. Both must be cited.

questions.questionHtml: In the Evidence Explained citation framework, what is the distinction between a 'repository' and a 'platform'?
options: They are synonyms — both refer to where a record is found online
The repository is the archive or institution that holds the original record; the platform is the digital service through which a digital image was accessed
The platform is for academic records; the repository is for government records
The repository is the physical location; the platform is the catalogue
questions.correctAnswer: The repository is the archive or institution that holds the original record; the platform is the digital service through which a digital image was accessed
questions.explanationHtml: A citation must identify both: the repository (e.g., General Register Office, Southport) where the original is held, and the platform (e.g., Ancestry, FindMyPast) through which a digital image was accessed. Citing only the platform omits essential information about the original source's provenance.

questions.questionHtml: You found a marriage entry by reading only a FindMyPast index transcription — you did not view the actual register image. How should this be reflected in your citation?
options: Cite it identically to a full image view — the information is the same
Note that the entry was found in an index transcription on FindMyPast and that the original register image was not personally examined
Do not cite it — index transcriptions are not valid genealogical sources
Treat it as a primary source since it is derived from an original record
questions.correctAnswer: Note that the entry was found in an index transcription on FindMyPast and that the original register image was not personally examined
questions.explanationHtml: A transcription may contain errors not present in the original. Citations must reflect how a source was accessed — viewing a digital image of the original is more reliable than reading a transcription. Adding 'transcription only; original register image not examined' signals to future researchers that this source should be verified against the original.

questions.questionHtml: Why is it important to include the date of access in citations for online genealogical sources?
options: Online genealogical sources are not considered valid unless a specific access date is provided
Online databases change — images are added, corrected, or removed; records are reindexed; and noting when access occurred enables assessment of which version was seen
The access date substitutes for the original record's date
It is a formality required by BCG but has no practical significance
questions.correctAnswer: Online databases change — images are added, corrected, or removed; records are reindexed; and noting when access occurred enables assessment of which version was seen
questions.explanationHtml: Online databases evolve continuously. A record visible on a specific date may be corrected, supplemented, or moved. Including the access date is not a formality — it contextualises what was seen and when, and it enables assessment of whether a subsequent change to the database affects the cited information.
